Text | Fanyu Meng

Editing | Er Mu, Fanyu Meng

We have all heard that strange change in sound as an ambulance races past. Why does it happen? Open your history textbook: search as hard as you like, you won’t find the answer, and you won’t manage to memorize it either. Relax, let me tell you: you’ve opened the wrong book. You need your high-school physics textbook! It’s the Doppler effect! Readers born after 1995 or 2000 may be a bit lost about what I’m on about: without even noticing, I’ve just used one song lyric to send everyone born in the ’80s straight back to the 2000s.

Today let’s chat about the Doppler effect. Unlike my earlier articles, this one has little to look at; it is mostly about listening. To celebrate the release of “Mojito,” the new single from Mandopop superstar Jay Chou, Jay will treat you all to a Doppler-flavored feast for the ears with his song “Listen to Your Mother.”

A friendly reminder: to protect your hearing, please turn down your headphone volume first.

Imagine a red dot that keeps yelling out sound. We’ll call it the source. It sits at [0,0], and you stand at [−5,0]. If neither you nor the source moves, the source speed is v=0, and the number of wavefronts reaching you each second stays the same: constant wavelength, constant frequency.

v=0, a stationary source [source: Wikipedia]

Now let the source move in the positive x direction. The wavefronts on the left spread out, so fewer of them reach you each second: the wavelength grows and the frequency drops. (c is the speed of sound.)

v<c, subsonic

The source hits the nitrous boost, floors it, and catches up with the speed of sound

v=c, transonic

Mid-sprint, the source glances back, sees a dog chasing it, and runs even faster

v>c, supersonic

I also touched on visualizing moving sources in an earlier article:

A history of acoustics: sound visualization, part 1

A small digression: the famous sound barrier appears when the source speed v approaches the speed of sound c.

The sound barrier made visible in the air around a plane approaching transonic speed [nl.pinterest.com]

Put the transonic animation above together with the diagram of sound propagation below (the blue lines in the animation above correspond to the black “wave” line where the black particles bunch up in the animation below). You can think of it as the sound waves “piling up” on top of one another. A small pocket of air is suddenly and strongly compressed and doesn’t disperse quickly, so water vapor condenses and the shock becomes visible. And because the energy is so concentrated, it produces a loud boom.

A source pushes the particles of the medium (air, for example) back and forth, sending the sound wave on its way

Back to the point.

To keep things serious, and to prove this really is popular science, here is a formula for appearances’ sake.

In the three animations above, where the source moves away from you, the frequency you hear as the listener is:

f=cc+vsf0

Here f is the frequency you hear, f0 is the frequency of the source, c is the speed of sound and v is the speed of the source, assumed constant. So the frequency you hear is lower than the source’s true frequency. If the source rushes toward you instead of away, just change the plus sign in the denominator to a minus, and the frequency you hear is higher than the source frequency. That is why an ambulance sounds higher as it approaches and lower once it has passed you.

Now for the main event. To demonstrate the Doppler effect, please give a big welcome to Chairman Chou (as fans call Jay Chou)!

Another friendly reminder: to protect your hearing, turn down your headphone volume before listening.

First, we put Chairman Chou in an ambulance and have him race past you at 120 km/h (ignoring wind), singing “Listen to Your Mother.”

Now Chairman Chou moves away from you at 300 km/h. He starts 1.5 m from you and moves perpendicular to the line between you.

Chairman Chou’s voice gets lower and lower, and quieter and quieter. Lower because of the frequency shift; quieter because of geometric spreading: if r is the distance between you, the sound pressure you receive falls off as 1/r. That attenuation gets in the way of going faster: any quicker, and in no time you won’t be able to hear what he’s singing at all. To bring out the frequency shift, we have decided to defy the laws of physics and throw out the 1/r! Here is what 300 km/h feels like without 1/r.

(Just as I got this far, WeChat suddenly informed me that I can upload at most three videos. Ten thousand expletives galloped through my mind. Luckily this is acoustics outreach, not video outreach: what matters is that you get to hear the sound.)

Again without 1/r, let’s see what happens when the source flees at the speed of sound

(*I couldn’t upload this audio to WeChat; it is in the Zhihu version of the article.)

The result: Chairman Chou gets more and more down.

What about twice the speed of sound? (Again ignoring 1/r.)

The lyrics are even harder to make out than usual.

The standard stuff is getting a bit dull. Time for something more exciting.

(At this point I was told I can only upload three audio clips as well. I nearly coughed up blood… my creative enthusiasm all but destroyed. Calm down, calm down, stay as professional as possible, and finish the article.)

Let’s hear what a guinea pig’s high-pitched squeak sounds like with the Doppler effect applied. Watch the video below and listen to the guinea pig from the 5-second mark.

Right. Take the audio from 5 seconds on. Now the guinea pig makes the same squeak, but while sprinting away from you at five times the speed of sound (6,120 km/h), again with no 1/r. What do you hear?

Behold: the guinea pig, digivolved to its Mega form.

Cover image: dhgate.com

Reference: Meng, Fanyu. Modeling of moving sound sources based on array measurements. PhD Dissertation, RWTH Aachen University, 2018.
